analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to approve every endangered-species listing or delisting before it takes effect.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor in the Congress's final weeks.
analysis.plain_summary: Right now, federal scientists at the Fish and Wildlife Service decide which animals and plants get listed as endangered or threatened, and businesses affected by a listing can challenge the decision in court. This bill would change that: no listing, removal, or status change could take effect until both the House and Senate pass, and the President signs, a joint resolution approving it. Because Congress rarely passes such resolutions, even well-supported listings would likely sit unapproved. The bill was introduced in the final weeks of the 117th Congress and died without any committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries that face restrictions on land use, drilling, mining, logging, or construction when a species is listed would benefit, because congressional approval would make new listings far less likely. Members of Congress would also gain a veto over decisions currently made by agency scientists.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Endangered Species Act so that a listing, removal from the list, or change in status of any species takes effect only upon enactment of a congressional joint resolution of approval [S3].
It covers all listing actions under Section 4(a) of the Act, meaning every addition, removal, or status change for endangered and threatened species would need an act of Congress [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Wildlife and the public would bear the cost: species awaiting protection would likely wait indefinitely if Congress does not act, weakening a program that has prevented extinctions. Congress also has almost never passed the kind of joint resolutions this would require, so the default would become no protection.

drawbacks.text: Supporters would argue that Congress, not unelected agency officials, should make decisions as consequential as listing a species, since listings can restrict how private land and public resources may be used; the bill's approval requirement is a straightforward application of that principle [S3].

The bill has no fallback if Congress fails to act: because a listing takes effect only upon enactment of a joint resolution [S3], a species blocked by inaction or gridlock would simply never receive protection, no matter the scientific evidence.

Congressional approval of individual listings would make each decision a target for intensive lobbying by affected industries, replacing a process with judicial review and public comment with one decided by legislators' political considerations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give Congress direct control over species listings, which its sponsor could argue increases accountability. But the design has a serious flaw: Congress routinely fails to pass joint resolutions of this kind, so the practical effect would be to stop most new listings rather than to review them, shifting protection decisions from scientists to whatever political coalition controls Congress at the moment. The cost to conservation would be large and one-sided.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House's last month and referred to the Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tracey Mann introduced the bill on November 29, 2022, in the final weeks of the 117th Congress [S5].
No member cosponsored it — the cosponsor list is empty [S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources on November 29, 2022, and the action record shows no hearing, markup, or committee vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public's existing species-protection system stayed intact: the bill's death means listings continue to be made by agency scientists subject to public comment and court review, rather than requiring an act of Congress for each species. No interest group gained anything concrete, because nothing happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Anyone who benefits from current species protections

for.name: Rep. Tracey Mann
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require congressional approval of endangered-species listing decisions.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: The House of Representatives
against.what_they_did: Never considered the bill on the floor; no bill ever reached a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no Democrat or Republican beyond the sponsor engaged with the bill, so no partisan split can be measured; it had zero cosponsors of either party [S4].

industries.note: A listing can restrict building on land where a protected species lives. Requiring Congress to approve every listing would make such restrictions far rarer, sparing developers compliance costs while leaving the public with weaker species protection.
Listed species can block or delay drilling, mining, and pipeline projects. Congressional approval of each listing would reduce the odds of new listings that constrain extraction.

Listings can limit pesticide use, grazing, and water withdrawals on farm and ranch land. The bill would make new constraints on agricultural operations less likely, but would shift the cost onto unprotected species and the ecosystem services they support.
